title: I Am the Hill
subtitle: The cowherds worship Govardhana, and Krishna accepts their offerings as the hill itself.
story:
Every year the cowherds of Vrindavan set aside a day for Indra, king of the gods, who sent the rain that kept their pastures green. This year, at the urging of a boy — Krishna, Nanda's son — they had set that day aside instead. They stood before Govardhana, the wide hill that rose from the plain and fed their cattle, and they prepared to honour the hill as they had once honoured the sky.

Krishna had argued that the hill was nearer to their lives than any distant god. Its grass nourished the cows; its slopes caught the clouds that watered the land; its shade sheltered the herds at noon. A sacrifice, he had said, should go to what actually keeps a people alive. Nanda, his father, had listened, and the cowherds had accepted the boy's words. What they were about to do, they did gladly.

It was a strange thing to do, and they knew it. For generations the sacrifice had gone upward, toward the gods in the sky. Now it went sideways, toward a hill they could touch and walk around and graze their cattle upon. But there was something steadying in it too. The hill asked for nothing and explained nothing. It stood before them, and they could circle it, and their animals could eat from it — and that, Krishna had told them, was worship enough.

So they brought offerings to the hill, and to the cows, and to the brahmins, honouring each in turn. It was a generous giving, the kind a festival calls for: food set out in abundance, gifts laid before the mountain. When the offerings had been made, the villagers climbed onto their decorated bullock carts and, with their cattle before them, began to walk around Govardhana, keeping the hill on their right as they made a slow, reverent circuit. It was an old gesture, this walking around a sacred thing, and it bound them to the hill as surely as the hill bound the clouds.

Then something happened that no one could have expected. Krishna, who had been walking among them like any cowherd boy, took on another form — a second self, vast and still — and stood upon the summit of the hill. "I am the hill," he said. And that form, the form that was the mountain, began to eat, taking in the abundant offerings the villagers had brought.

The people of Vrindavan, seeing the embodied mountain before them, fell still with wonder. They bowed low, and a murmur passed among them: "Behold, the hill has favoured us." They had offered their sacrifice to a heap of earth and stone, and the earth and stone had answered — as though, for that one moment, the mountain and the boy who had led them to it were one.
reflection: The villagers set out to honor a hill and found themselves answered, a moment that quietly turns the ordinary order of sacrifice on its head: the worshipper speaks, and the object of worship, which should be silent, speaks back.
next_story_tease: But Indra had been watching, and he was not prepared to let the insult pass.
hero_scene: Krishna, having taken on a second vast form, standing upon the summit of Govardhana and receiving the cowherds' offerings as the hill itself, while the villagers below bow low and their decorated bullock carts and cattle ring the mountain.
visual_elements: Krishna in two forms, the second vast and still on the hilltop
Govardhana hill rising from the plain
